title: SEMCOG Rain Gauge Network 2003 Annual Report

SEMCOG Rain Gauge Network 2003 Annual Report

July 2004. © SEMCOG 2004.

SEMCOG, the Southeast Michigan Council of Governments. Local Governments Advancing Southeast Michigan.

Abstract

This document reports annual precipitation amounts of the SEMCOG Rain Gauge Network for 2003, annual departures from median amounts, calculated probabilities, and annual changes from 2002. The 65-gauge network is operated by SEMCOG, with expert guidance provided by Dr. Fred Nurnberger, climatology consultant (contact Anne Ordiway, 517-394-0007).

Preparation of this document was financed by contributions from the Rain Gauge Network partners — City of Detroit, Livingston County, Macomb County, Wayne County, and SEMCOG.

Permission is granted to cite portions of this publication, with proper attribution. The first source attribution must be “SEMCOG, the Southeast Michigan Council of Governments.” Subsequently, “SEMCOG” is sufficient. Reprinting in any form must include the publication’s full title page.

Southeast Michigan Council of Governments, Information Services, 535 Griswold Street, Suite 300, Detroit, MI 48226-3602. 313-961-4266; fax 313-961-4869. www.semcog.org; infoservices@semcog.org. $10.00.

Mission

SEMCOG’s mission is solving regional planning problems — improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the region’s local governments as well as the quality of life in Southeast Michigan. Essential functions are:

  • providing a forum for addressing issues which extend beyond individual governmental boundaries by fostering collaborative regional planning, and
  • facilitating intergovernmental relations among local governments and state and federal agencies.

As a regional planning partnership in Southeast Michigan, SEMCOG is accountable to local governments who join as members. Membership is open to all counties, cities, villages, townships, intermediate school districts, and community colleges in Livingston, Macomb, Monroe, Oakland, St. Clair, Washtenaw, and Wayne Counties.

Responsibilities

SEMCOG’s primary activities support local planning through use of SEMCOG’s technical, data, and intergovernmental resources. In collaboration with local governments, SEMCOG has responsibility for adopting regionwide plans and policies for community and economic development, water and air quality, land use, and transportation, including approval of state and federal transportation projects. Funding for SEMCOG is provided by federal and state grants, contracts, and membership fees.

Policy decision making

All SEMCOG policy decisions are made by local elected officials, ensuring that regional policies reflect the interests of member communities. Participants serve on one or both of the policymaking bodies — the General Assembly and the Executive Committee.

Prior to policy adoption, technical advisory councils provide the structure for gaining input on transportation, environment, community and economic development, data analysis, and education. This deliberative process includes broad-based representation from local governments, the business community, environmental organizations, and other special interest and citizen groups.

2003 Summary of Annual Precipitation for the SEMCOG Recording Rain Gauge Network

Annual precipitation totals across the SEMCOG network during 2003 ranged from a high of 38.48 inches at A-05 in east-central Washtenaw County to a low of 24.17 inches at W-42 in northeastern Wayne County (Figure 1 and Tables 1 and 3). Only seven additional gauges recorded more than 34 inches, namely: two in southwest Livingston County (36.19 inches at L-10 and 34.15 inches at L-05); two in central Washtenaw County (35.40 inches at A-03 and 34.74 inches at A-01); two in southeast Oakland County (35.00 inches at O-02 and 34.52 inches at O-18); two in southeastern Wayne County (31.91 inches at W-45 and 30.91 inches at W-35, respectively); and one in southern Macomb County (34.41 inches at M-03). The regions of lowest precipitation (i.e., less than 28 inches) included: east-central (two gauges) and southeastern (one gauge) Macomb County; west-central to northeast central (four gauges) Oakland County; and northeast and east-central (six gauges) Wayne County. It should be noted that four of the six gauges in Wayne County were roof-exposure locations.

Annual precipitation departures from long-term median amounts [(for stations in the network with more than 15 years of record through 2000] (Figure 2) were mostly below the median (47 of 68 gauges, or 69 percent). Values ranged from an above-median 8.00 inches at A-05 in east-central Washtenaw County to a below-median value of 9.14 inches at W-42 in northeast Wayne County. Only three additional stations were more than four inches below the median. In general, the region extending south of a line from northwestern Livingston County to southeastern Wayne County, the southeastern area of Oakland County, and northeastern Macomb County were all above the median. The remainder of the five-county area was below the median, with isolated stations slightly above the median (about one half-inch).

Figure 3 shows the percentile ranking of each annual station total compared to historical data through 2000, based on a gamma probability distribution function. The map values represent the decimal fraction of years that total annual precipitation at that station would have been less than or equal to the 2003 amount. For example, the 0.8 isoline encloses all stations in the area where the annual amount would be less than or equal to that received in 2003 during eight years in 10. The complement of that value, .2, means that during only two years in 10 should a station be expected to record more rain than was recorded in 2003. Care must be used in interpreting the values, however, because of the relatively short periods-of-record, as short as 16 years for some stations. The widely varied nature of the precipitation amounts and departures from the median amount is reflected in the widely disparate calculated probabilities. As expected, only those areas with positive departures from the median had probabilities greater than 0.50. The highest probability value was .95 at A-05, with the others being in the range of 0.60 to 0.83. The extreme low values were at stations in northeastern and east-central Wayne County, southeastern Macomb County, and southwestern Oakland County, where calculated values were between 0.03 and 0.15. Two additional stations, one in northeastern Wayne County and one in northeastern Oakland County, showed a probability of 0.18.

Comparatively, the SEMCOG network was much wetter in 2003 than in 2002 (Figure 4). The greatest changes were recorded in southwestern Livingston County and northwest-to-southeast Oakland County, where totals were more than eight inches above the 2002 values. The extreme changes were +11.07 inches at A-02 and +10.25 inches at L-05. Totals for four nearby stations in southern Livingston County and four in northwest-to-southeast-central Oakland County were more than eight inches greater than in 2002. Two gauges in each of these counties increased nine inches or more, with the two in Livingston County nearing 10 inches (+9.95 inches at L-11 and +9.93 inches at L-10). An area centered along a southwest-to-northeast line from southwestern Livingston County to central Oakland County was more than six inches wetter than in 2002. Only six stations were drier than in 2002; -0.90 inches at M-03 in southeastern Macomb County was the greatest negative change from 2002 to 2003.

In summary, 2003 was a highly varied year; some areas were very wet and others very dry. For many residents of the five-county area, the change was even more noticeable following the relatively dry year of 2002.

The original narrative lists W-45 as 31.91 inches and W-35 as 30.91 inches while discussing gauges above 34 inches. The 2003 data table gives W-45 as 31.44 inches and W-35 as 32.70 inches. The narrative wording is retained as printed.

Higher totals occur in southwest Livingston, central Washtenaw and southeast Oakland. The Table 1 station totals below preserve exact annual numbers.

Figure 2: 2003 annual departure from median

2003 Annual departure from median

Forty-seven of 68 gauges (69 percent) were below their historical median. A-05 was 8.00 inches above median; W-42 was 9.14 inches below. Above-median areas generally lie south of a line from northwestern Livingston to southeastern Wayne, plus southeast Oakland and northeast Macomb. Most remaining areas were below median.

The map covers Livingston, Oakland, Macomb, Washtenaw and Wayne Counties. Crosses locate rain gauges; asterisks mark roof-exposure gauges. Black contour lines connect equal values.

Related station annual totals for 2003

Figure 3: Calculated probabilities, 2003 annual precipitation

2003 Calculated annual precipitation probabilities

The map gives the estimated fraction of years whose annual precipitation would be at or below the 2003 total, based on a gamma distribution and historical data through 2000. A-05 is highest at 0.95. Other above-median areas are generally 0.60–0.83. Low values of 0.03–0.15 occur in northeastern/east-central Wayne, southeastern Macomb and southwestern Oakland; two additional stations are 0.18. Values are dimensionless probabilities, not inches. Records as short as 16 years limit interpretation.

The map covers Livingston, Oakland, Macomb, Washtenaw and Wayne Counties. Crosses locate rain gauges; asterisks mark roof-exposure gauges. Black contour lines connect equal values.

Related station annual totals for 2003

Figure 4: 2003 annual precipitation change from 2002

2003 Annual precipitation change from 2002

The region was generally wetter than 2002. A-02 increased 11.07 inches; L-05, 10.25; L-11, 9.95; and L-10, 9.93. A band from southwestern Livingston to central Oakland was over 6 inches wetter. Only six stations were drier; the largest decrease was 0.90 inches at M-03. Positive numbers mean more precipitation than 2002.

The map covers Livingston, Oakland, Macomb, Washtenaw and Wayne Counties. Crosses locate rain gauges; asterisks mark roof-exposure gauges. Black contour lines connect equal values.

Related station annual totals for 2003

Figure 5: SEMCOG active stations, June 2004

Active stations in June 2004

The map locates SEMCOG rain gauges across five counties in southeastern Michigan: Livingston in the northwest, Oakland to its east, Macomb in the northeast, Washtenaw in the southwest, and Wayne in the southeast. County boundaries are drawn as black lines. Each gauge is labeled with its station code. Crosses mark gauge locations and asterisks identify roof-exposure locations.

Station prefixes visible on the map are A, L, M, O and W. The source does not give coordinates or street addresses; these cannot be recovered exactly from the printed map alone.
